:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Given that $f(x) = \dfrac 1 {x^3}$ and that $F'(x) = f(x)$, calculate $F(x)$.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if

$$
F'(x) = f(x)
$$

then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
F^{′}(x) &= f(x) \\
\intF^{′}(x)dx &= \intf(x)dx \\
F(x) &= \intf(x)dx
\end{aligned}
$$

Note that

$$
\dfrac 1 {x^3}= x^{-3}
$$

So, we can use the power rule with $n=-3$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}
F(x) &= \intf(x)dx \\
&= \int\frac{1}{x^{3}}dx \\
&= \intx^{-3}dx \\
&= \frac{x^{-3 + 1}}{-3 + 1} + C \\
&=-\frac{x^{-2}}{2} + C \\
&=-\frac{1}{2x^{2}} + C
\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Given that $f(x) = x^{-2/3}$ and that $F^{′}(x) = f(x)$, calculate $F(x)$.
Given that $f(x) = \frac{1}{x^{3/5}}$ and that $F^{′}(x) = f(x)$, calculate $F(x)$.

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if ${F}^{'}(x)=f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{'}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{'}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $\frac{1}{{x}^{4/3}}={x}^{-4/3}.$ So, we can use the power rule with $n=-\frac{4}{3}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{-4/3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-4/3+1}}{(-\frac{4}{3}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-1/3}}{(-\frac{1}{3})}+C \\  & =-3{x}^{-1/3}+C \\  & =-\frac{3}{{x}^{1/3}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $\frac{1}{{x}^{4}}={x}^{-4}.$ So, we can use the power rule with $n=-4$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x & =\int {x}^{-4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-4+1}}{-4+1}+C \\  & =-\frac{{x}^{-3}}{3}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{3{x}^{3}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{5}}}=\frac{1}{{x}^{5/2}}={x}^{-5/2}.$ So, we can use the power rule with $n=-\frac{5}{2}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{5}}} & =\int {x}^{-5/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-5/2+1}}{-\frac{5}{2}+1}+C \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}{x}^{-3/2}+C \\  & =-\frac{2}{3{x}^{3/2}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if ${F}^{'}(x)=f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{'}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{'}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can use the power rule with $n=-\frac{1}{7}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{-1/7}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-1/7+1}}{(-\frac{1}{7}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{6/7}}{(\frac{6}{7})}+C \\  & =\frac{7}{6}{x}^{6/7}+C.\end{aligned}
$$
